title: Zod and a validate() middleware exist and cover 7 of 285 write routes, all of them auth
evidence: The stack is Zod (^4.3.5 in package.json), a shared `validate(schema, source)` middleware (middleware/validate.js) that emits VALIDATION_ERROR through sendErrorResponse with per-field details, plus schema modules in shared/schemas/auth-schemas.js, shared/zod-schemas.js and validation/. No Joi, no express-validator (0 files). Actual adoption: `validate(<Schema>)` appears on exactly 7 route declarations, at auth-health.js:60, :113, :116, :119, :130, :178 and auth-provider.js:34. Of the 285 write-route declarations in routes/+controllers/ (205 POST, 31 PUT, 21 PATCH, 28 DELETE), 7 use a declarative schema, 144 do their own ad-hoc checking inside the handler body, and 135 have neither a schema nor a 400 branch in the route body. Spot-reading the highest-risk of those 135 shows the safety usually does exist one layer down and is real — credit-notes POST (routes/api/finance/credit-notes.js:54) hands raw body fields to creditNoteService.createCreditNote, which validates and caps them (credit-note-service.js:219-268, :336); site-analyses PUT /:id passes req.body wholesale but siteAnalysisService.updateAnalysis whitelists 24 fields and excludes passedCriteria/verifiedBy/verifiedAt/farmId/organizationId (site-analysis-service.js:127-141). So the gap is not 'unvalidated' — it is 'unvalidated at the boundary, ad hoc below it, and invisible to the OpenAPI spec'.
impact: The 48-operation OpenAPI spec (7.4% of the surface) is the only machine-readable statement of what a request body may contain, and for 278 of 285 write routes there is no schema object that a spec generator, a test, or an integrator could read. Each of the 144 hand-rolled guards is a separate place for a check to be forgotten; the boundary contract is unenumerable.
fix: Do not schema all 285. Put the existing middleware on the doors where a wrong body has consequences that outlive the request: the money writes (routes/api/finance/credit-notes.js:54, debit-notes, refunds, manual-journal-entries) and the identity writes (routes/api/admin/users.js:367,:568,:598). Pattern is already proven in-repo — `router.post('/', authenticateProvider, validate(createCreditNoteSchema), handler)` — and each schema is ~10 lines next to shared/schemas/auth-schemas.js. That is ~12 routes in 6 files and it makes those bodies expressible in the OpenAPI spec. Sweep the rest per domain as follow-up.
verdict_reason: Counts reproduce exactly: 285 write-route declarations in routes/+controllers/ split 205 POST / 31 PUT / 21 PATCH / 28 DELETE, and `validate(<Schema>)` appears on exactly 7 declarations at auth-health.js:60,:113,:116,:119,:130,:178 and auth-provider.js:34. zod ^4.3.5 in package.json, no joi or express-validator. middleware/validate.js:22-40 does emit VALIDATION_ERROR through sendErrorResponse with per-field details. The credit-notes door does hand raw body fields straight to the service (routes/api/finance/credit-notes.js:53-64) and the service does validate/cap them (credit-note-service.js:210-275, :331-363), so the 'ad hoc below the boundary' characterisation is accurate and the finding is honest about it.
correction: The 144 hand-rolled / 135 neither split was not recomputed here — treat those two sub-numbers as unverified. The proposed target line is routes/api/finance/credit-notes.js:53 (the router.post declaration), not :54.

title: Two rate-limiter implementations disagree on header namespace, body shape and Retry-After — and the money endpoints are the ones missing it
evidence: Ran both. express-rate-limit (globalLimiter and the five auth limiters, server.js:229-260) emits `ratelimit-limit` / `ratelimit-remaining` / `ratelimit-reset` and sets `Retry-After: 900` before the handler (dist/index.cjs:993-995). The hand-rolled createRateLimiter (middleware/rate-limiter.js) emits `X-RateLimit-Limit` / `-Remaining` / `-Reset` (:121-123) and its 429 at :128-133 carries `retryAfterSeconds` in the JSON body with NO Retry-After header — verified by running the real module behind /api/payments/checkout: `status=429 Retry-After=null x-ratelimit-limit=1`. That hand-rolled limiter is exactly what guards /api/payments/create, /phase1, /phase2 and /checkout (server.js:275-286) plus POST /api/consumer-feedback (consumer-feedback.js:22-26). The 429 bodies differ three ways across the codebase: `{success,error,message,retryAfterSeconds}` (rate-limiter.js:128), `{success,code,error,requestId}` (server.js:220-226), and a bare text/html string (globalLimiter, see ERR-01).
impact: A client cannot read one header to learn its budget, and the four endpoints where correct back-off matters most — the ones that mint Stripe PaymentIntents — are the four that omit the standard header every HTTP client library already knows how to honour. A retry loop on checkout will hammer rather than wait.
fix: In middleware/rate-limiter.js, add one line before the 429 return at :128: `res.setHeader('Retry-After', Math.ceil((resetTime - now) / 1000));`. Same call already computes that number for the body. Second line, for header parity with the other limiter: also set `RateLimit-Limit`/`RateLimit-Remaining`/`RateLimit-Reset` alongside the X- forms at :121-123, keeping the X- ones so nothing that reads them breaks.
verdict_reason: Both implementations read. middleware/rate-limiter.js:121-123 sets X-RateLimit-Limit/-Remaining/-Reset and the 429 at :127-134 returns {success,error,message,retryAfterSeconds} with no Retry-After header — grep for 'Retry-After' in that file returns nothing, only the body field at :132. express-rate-limit's side verified live: ratelimit-limit header plus `retry-after: 900`. That hand-rolled limiter is what guards the money doors (paymentLimiter mounted on /api/payments/create, /phase1, /phase2, /checkout) and the public feedback POST. The one-line setHeader fix is correct and touches nothing else.
correction: Path/line refs are stale: the payment mounts are at server.js:337-343 (not :275-286) and the feedback limiter is routes/api/integration/consumer-feedback.js:22-26 (the finding drops the /integration segment). The 429 body site is rate-limiter.js:128-133 as stated.

title: One 1000-per-15-min bucket per IP covers reads and writes alike across the whole API
evidence: `rate=1000` came back on all 22 sampled responses, read and write paths alike — that is globalLimiter's default `max: parsePositiveInt(process.env.RATE_LIMIT_MAX, 1000)` over a 15-minute window, mounted `app.use('/api', globalLimiter)` at :239. The only routes with a narrower budget are the eight explicit prefixes registered at :249-263 and :275-286 (auth login/register/check-identifier/reset-password, the IdP prefix, four payment paths and /api/callbacks). Everything else — all 205 POST, 31 PUT, 21 PATCH and 28 DELETE handlers outside those prefixes, plus all 363 GETs — shares one bucket keyed purely on `getRequestIp(req)`. 1000/15 min is 1.1 requests per second sustained, per source IP, for every user behind that IP.
impact: No read/write class split: a scripted POST loop against an application-mutation door draws from the same budget as a dashboard poll, so neither is sized for its own risk. And because the key is the raw IP, one shared connection is one budget — a district office or a farmer co-operative NAT'd behind a single address shares 1.1 req/s among everyone in the building, and the whole building gets 429'd together (with a text/html body — see ERR-01). No measurement of real per-page request counts was taken, so I cannot state how many concurrent users trip it; that is an open question worth a browser-tab measurement.
fix: Smallest correct version: keep the global bucket as the outer ceiling and add one write-class limiter in front of the mutating surface, reusing the express-rate-limit instance already in the file — `const writeLimiter = rateLimit({ windowMs: 60_000, max: parsePositiveInt(process.env.RATE_LIMIT_WRITE_MAX, 60), standardHeaders: true, legacyHeaders: false, keyGenerator: req => getRequestIp(req), skip: req => ['GET','HEAD','OPTIONS'].includes(req.method), handler: authRateLimitHandler('Too many write requests. Please slow down.') });` mounted `app.use('/api', writeLimiter)` right after :239. Separately, once a real logged-in identity exists the key should be the user id rather than the IP for authenticated traffic, which removes the shared-NAT cliff — but that has to go after the limiters, so it is a follow-up, not part of this change.
verdict_reason: Confirmed: globalLimiter `max: parsePositiveInt(process.env.RATE_LIMIT_MAX, 1000)` over a 15-min window, keyGenerator `req => getRequestIp(req)`, mounted `app.use('/api', globalLimiter)` — one per-IP bucket in front of essentially the whole surface. 1000/900s = 1.11 req/s is arithmetically right, and the shared-NAT consequence follows from the raw-IP key. The finding correctly refuses to guess how many concurrent users trip it.
correction: Line refs are server.js:239-246 + mount at :293, not 229-239. 'Only eight explicit prefixes' undercounts: the auth limiters are registered on BOTH /api and /api/v1 in the loop at :276-296, the payment/webhook mounts are at :337-344, and consumer-feedback carries its own route-local createRateLimiter (10/min) at routes/api/integration/consumer-feedback.js:22-26. Also the proposed writeLimiter omits `skip: shouldSkipAuthRateLimit`, which every other limiter in the file carries (server.js:255, :283, …) — without it the jest suites, seed scripts and CI would start collecting 429s. Add that skip before proposing it.

title: Any http://127.0.0.1 port is a credentialed CORS origin in production, and localhost sits in the production allowlist
evidence: The origin callback returns `callback(null, true)` for any origin matching `normalizedOrigin.startsWith('http://127.0.0.1:')` (server.js:197, commented "for IDE proxy testing") with no environment guard — it applies when NODE_ENV is production exactly as in development. The surrounding cors() call sets `credentials: true` (:203). Separately, productionDefaultOrigins (:156-162) is `https://gacpth.com`, `https://www.gacpth.com`, `https://admin.gacpth.com`, `http://localhost:3000`, `https://localhost` — two loopback entries carried into the production set. A request with no Origin header is also allowed unconditionally (:194). One deliberate wildcard exists and is correctly scoped: /api/trace is `origin: '*'` but GET/OPTIONS only and without credentials (:181-186).
impact: Anything the victim is running on their own loopback — a dev server, a local tool, a downloaded app that opens a port — can make credentialed cross-origin calls to the production API and read the responses, because the browser will attach the auth cookie and the server will echo the allow-origin. Narrow (it needs something on the user's 127.0.0.1) but it is a production allowance made for IDE convenience, on a platform whose three-domain split memo says gacpth.com must not be publicly open.
fix: Gate the loopback branch on non-production and drop the two localhost entries from the production defaults. At :197: `if (!isProduction && normalizedOrigin.startsWith('http://127.0.0.1:')) { return callback(null, true); }`, and delete `'http://localhost:3000'` and `'https://localhost'` from productionDefaultOrigins (:160-161). Developers keep them through developmentDefaultOrigins (:164-169) and through CORS_ORIGIN/CORS_ORIGINS env entries, which are already merged in at :171-177.
verdict_reason: Verified in the current file: `if (normalizedOrigin.startsWith('http://127.0.0.1:')) { return callback(null, true); }` with the '(for IDE proxy testing)' comment and no environment guard, inside the cors() call that sets `credentials: true`; productionDefaultOrigins is exactly the five entries quoted, including 'http://localhost:3000' and 'https://localhost'; a missing Origin is allowed unconditionally one line above; /api/trace's `origin:'*'` is GET/OPTIONS-only without credentials. developmentDefaultOrigins plus the CORS_ORIGIN/CORS_ORIGINS/FRONTEND_URL/… merge do preserve the developer's loopback access, so the proposed fix costs developers nothing.
correction: Line numbers shifted by fe289fea (which rewrote the deny branch to callback(null,false)): the loopback branch is server.js:196, credentials:true at :211, no-origin allow at :193, productionDefaultOrigins :156-162 (unchanged), /api/trace :182-187.

title: Two write doors into SystemConfig with different coercion, no key allowlist, and no shape check on the pricing row
evidence: PATCH /api/admin/config/:key upserts with `value: String(value)` on both the update and create branches (config.js:43, :48), where `value` comes straight from `req.body` destructuring at :36 with no presence check — an absent field makes `String(undefined)` and stores the literal four-character string `"undefined"`. `key` is taken from the path with no allowlist, so any key can be created. `type` is set only on the create branch, so changing a value never corrects a wrong type. The second door, PUT /api/system-config/:key (mounted at routes/api/index.js line for /system-config; handler at system-config-controller.js:100-111), writes `value` with no coercion at all. Consumption is unguarded in the same way: systemConfigService.getValue JSON.parses and falls back to the raw string on failure (system-config-service.js:38-48), and routes/api/finance/pricing.js:231 and :254 do `const fees = stored || defaultFeesPayload()` — a stored `"undefined"` string is truthy, so GET /api/pricing and GET /api/pricing/fees would serve it verbatim as the fee table.
impact: One admin PATCH with a mistyped body name silently replaces the public fee table with a string, and both pricing endpoints return `{success: true, data: "undefined"}` with a 200. The binding invoice math is safe — it runs through fee-service via buildEstimateBreakdown, not through this row — so the blast radius is the fee a Thai government platform DISPLAYS to applicants, not the fee it charges. Two doors with different coercion into the same column also means a value's stored form depends on which screen wrote it.
fix: Two changes, both small. (1) In config.js:33, refuse an absent value before the upsert: `if (value === undefined || value === null) { return sendErrorResponse(res, req, { status: 400, code: 'VALIDATION_ERROR', message: 'value is required' }); }` and move `type` into the update branch so a correction takes. (2) In routes/api/finance/pricing.js:231 and :254, require the parsed value to be the shape the page needs before trusting it: `const fees = (stored && typeof stored === 'object' && !Array.isArray(stored)) ? stored : defaultFeesPayload();` — the defaults already exist at defaultFeesPayload(). Retiring one of the two write doors is a bigger call and belongs to the operator; flag it rather than pick.
verdict_reason: Verified line by line: routes/api/admin/config.js:33 `router.patch('/:key')`, :36 destructures value/type/description with no presence check, :43 and :48 both write `value: String(value)`, `type` set only on the create branch, key taken from the path with no allowlist. Second door confirmed mounted: routes/api/system/system-config-routes.js:14 → system-config-controller.js:100-111 writing `value` uncoerced. system-config-service.js:36-48 JSON.parses and falls back to the raw string; routes/api/finance/pricing.js:231-232 and :254-255 do `const fees = stored || defaultFeesPayload()`, and grep shows those two endpoints are the ONLY readers of the 'pricing_fees' key — so the stated blast radius (displayed fees, not billed amounts) is right.
correction: Three refinements. (a) The fees fallback lines are :232 and :255 (:231/:254 are the getValue calls). (b) SystemConfig.value is a String column (prisma/schema/system.prisma:54), so the uncoerced door cannot store a non-string — Prisma rejects it — which narrows 'the stored form depends on which screen wrote it' to String()-coercion of numbers/booleans, not arbitrary JSON. (c) Both doors are admin-gated (routes/api/admin/index.js:7-8 authenticateProvider + requireAdmin; system-config-routes.js:14 authenticateProvider + adminOnly), so the trigger is an admin typo, not an anonymous request — worth saying, because it is what keeps this 'consistency' and not 'critical'.

title: Tenant resolution cannot tell 'claim present and null' from 'legacy token', so org-less users pay a wasted query on every request
evidence: The JWT already carries the claim: prisma-auth-service.js:518 signs `organizationId: user.organizationId || null`. resolveOrganizationId branches on truthiness — `if (reqUser.organizationId) { return reqUser.organizationId; }` at :34 — and otherwise falls through to `prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id: reqUser.id }, select: { organizationId: true } })` at :41, whose comment says the fallback is "Legacy token without the claim". But a current token for a user whose User.organizationId is NULL also lands there, on every single request, and the query returns null every single time. I could not query the live database to count how many users that is, so the size of the affected population is an open question, not a claim.
impact: For each affected user, a third sequential 244 ms Sydney round trip on every authenticated request, on top of the two in AUTH-01, for a lookup whose answer is structurally guaranteed to be null. If it is a common state the median grows by a quarter-second; if it is rare, the fix still costs one line.
fix: Distinguish the two cases by key presence rather than truthiness. At tenant-context-middleware.js:34: `if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(reqUser, 'organizationId')) { return reqUser.organizationId || null; }` — a current token always has the key (set at prisma-auth-service.js:518, null or not) and short-circuits; a pre-claim legacy token lacks it and still takes the DB fallback at :41, so the legacy path the comment describes keeps working unchanged.
verdict_reason: Verified: prisma-auth-service.js:518 signs `organizationId: user.organizationId || null` into every access token, auth-middleware.js:519 spreads `...decoded` into req.user so the key survives, and tenant-context-middleware.js:34 branches on truthiness — a present-but-null claim falls through to the `prisma.user.findUnique` at :41-44 whose comment calls it the legacy path. For an org-less user that query returns null on every authenticated request, on the same 452-route path as AUTH-01. The hasOwnProperty fix distinguishes the two cases correctly and preserves the pre-claim legacy fallback.
correction: One factual fix and one open item. The module doc comment at :20-22 says an org-less user is 'rejected with 500'; the code does not — tenantContextMiddleware:61-67 calls next() without a tenant scope. Correct that stale comment in the same one-line change. And as the finding itself concedes, the affected population is unmeasured, so the impact is 'one wasted round trip per request for however many users have User.organizationId NULL', not a claimed median shift.

title: ON DELETE SET NULL on invoices.applicationId and checkout_orders.applicationId is forbidden by a CHECK on the same table — two unsatisfiable rules on the two live money tables
evidence: Both Prisma relations are optional with NO explicit onDelete (billing.prisma:17 `application Application? @relation(fields: [applicationId], references: [id])`, billing.prisma:1297 same shape), so Prisma emitted its default for an optional relation: SET NULL. I read both DDLs. invoices: `ADD CONSTRAINT invoices_applicationId_fkey ... ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE` (drift migration:653; the preceding unconditional `DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS` at :30 means this replaces the original RESTRICT from 20260110020726:892). The same table carries `invoices_billable_xor_chk CHECK ((applicationId IS NOT NULL AND subscriptionId IS NULL) OR (applicationId IS NULL AND subscriptionId IS NOT NULL))`. checkout_orders is identical: FK `ON DELETE SET NULL` at :176-177, `checkout_orders_target_xor_check` at :72-76. billing.prisma:14-16 states the intent in prose: "Exactly one of {applicationId, subscriptionId} must be set; the DB enforces this with a CHECK constraint."
impact: For every application-billed invoice or checkout order — i.e. all of them, since subscriptions are unused — the FK's declared action can never execute. `DELETE FROM applications WHERE id=$1` aborts with SQLSTATE 23514 (check_violation on invoices_billable_xor_chk) rather than a clean 23503 foreign_key_violation, so the error names the wrong table and the wrong reason. Worse is the intent gap: the schema author believes deleting an application is RESTRICTed by its money rows; nothing in the schema says so, and the only thing standing between an application delete and a set of orphaned revenue rows is a CHECK constraint that was written for a different purpose. Reachable today only from ops scripts (scripts/cleanup-uat.js:42, scripts/revert-accidental-seed-2026-08-26.js:192) and the env-gated e2e router (routes/api/index.js:81), which is exactly when a confusing error costs the most.
verdict_reason: Reproduced end-to-end. Masked DATABASE_URL inspection confirms gacp-backend and gacp-backend-demo both point at aws-1-ap-southeast-2.pooler.supabase.com:5432 with NO query params (Supavisor session mode), while gacp-backend-staging is aws-0-ap-northeast-2:6543?pgbouncer=true. prisma-database.js:74-77 confirmed: POOL_SIZE = parseInt(process.env.PRISMA_POOL_SIZE,10) || 20, POOL_TIMEOUT || 15, appended as connection_limit/pool_timeout. Firing 20 concurrent SELECT 1 from inside gacp-backend with connection_limit=20 produced the exact error verbatim: 'FATAL: (EMAXCONNSESSION) max clients reached in session mode - max clients are limited to pool_size: 15'. max_connections=60 confirmed; Supavisor client backends counted live (11 at my sample: 10 idle + 1 active).
correction: Two numbers to tighten. (1) My repro failed 15 of 20 (elapsed 4570ms, ok 5), not 'index 15 onward' — because the two running containers already hold session slots, so the app-visible ceiling is well below 15 spare. That makes the finding understated, not overstated. (2) The file locations are prisma-database.js:74-77 (POOL_SIZE:74, POOL_TIMEOUT:75, poolParams:76, pooledUrl:77), not 74-79. The pool_size:15 ceiling is per Supabase project, shared by both containers plus any psql/migration, which is exactly the point the fix makes.

title: The quote→invoice mint has neither a transaction nor an idempotency key, and Invoice.quoteId has an index but no unique — a failed second write lets the same quote mint a second tax invoice
evidence: `createInvoiceFromQuote` does `const invoice = await prisma.invoice.create({ data })` (quote-service.js:347) then, as a separate statement, `await prisma.invoiceLineItem.createMany({...})` (:358) — no $transaction wraps them (the comment at :335-346 explains why they cannot be a nested write, but does not put them in a transaction either). Both callers then update the quote in a THIRD unwrapped statement: quotes-provider-routes.js:56 `await quoteService.updateStatus(quote.id, 'invoiced')` and finance/quotes.js:284 `await quoteService.markAcceptedWithInvoice(id, invoice.id)`. The only guard against a repeat mint is the status read at quotes-provider-routes.js:37 / finance/quotes.js:257. Schema: `quoteId String?` + `quote Quote? @relation(...)` (billing.prisma:22-23) and `@@index([quoteId])` (:159) — there is no @@unique.
impact: Two concrete failures. (a) invoice.create commits, invoiceLineItem.createMany fails → a tax invoice exists carrying subtotal/vat/totalAmount with zero line items; ม.86/4 requires the itemisation, and the FlowAccount XLSX export reads lineItems. (b) invoice.create commits, the quote status update fails → the quote is still 'accepted'/'sent', so pressing the button again mints a SECOND invoice with a different unique number for the same quote and the same money. Nothing at the DB level refuses it. The newer checkout path already solved exactly this: CheckoutDocument carries `@@unique([checkoutOrderId, documentType])` (billing.prisma:1507) and settlement carries the partial unique index `journal_entries_settlement_once` (migrations/20260816084713_settlement_resilience/migration.sql:15-17). The legacy quote path was left without either.
verdict_reason: Latency constant reproduced independently: 7x SELECT 1 from inside gacp-backend = 245.7/245.7/245.8/245.8/245.8/245.8/245.9ms, median 245.8; 3 sequential = 737.5ms = exactly 3x. Loopback timings on gacp-backend-demo: /api/health 515/263/301ms, /api/system-config/public 548/313/309ms — one round trip plus small app time, no nginx/Cloudflare involved. pg_stat_statements totals now 437,645 calls / 485,430ms, matching the finding's 437,077 / 484s. Direction and conclusion are right.
correction: Three corrections. (1) Location is wrong: pooledUrl is prisma-database.js:77, not :99. (2) The headline arithmetic is inflated by about a third. Of the 437,645 statements, roughly 145k are Supavisor/pooler-internal and are NOT app round trips from Singapore: 'SELECT * FROM pgbouncer.get_auth($1)' 112,897 calls, DISCARD ALL 11,422, DEALLOCATE ALL 14,310, SHOW transaction_read_only 6,580. The honest figure is ~292k app statements x 245.8ms = ~20 hours of wire against 485s of DB work, ratio ~148:1, not 30.2 hours / 224:1. (3) '100% of server latency is the wire' overstates: /api/health on loopback measured 263-515ms against a 245.8ms RTT, so 7-20% is app time. Everything else — the region diagnosis, the per-endpoint round-trip decomposition, and the list of what the move does NOT fix — holds.

title: Invoice numbers on the provider quote→invoice route come from count()+1, and count() is soft-delete-filtered — soft-deleting one invoice makes the next same-day number collide with an existing one
evidence: `async generateInvoiceNumberSequential() { const dateStr = ...; const count = await prisma.invoice.count(); return `INV-${dateStr}${(count+1).toString().padStart(4,'0')}`; }` (quote-service.js:380-384). Two facts make this unsafe rather than merely ugly: (a) `count` is in the soft-delete extension's filtered operation list (services/soft-delete-extension.js:189) and `Invoice` is in SOFT_DELETE_MODELS (:63), so count() returns live rows only and DECREASES when an invoice is soft-deleted; (b) `invoiceNumber String @unique` (billing.prisma:10). The canonical allocator already exists and does this correctly — receipt-numbering-service.js allocates from the ReceiptSequence table inside a serializable transaction and throws RECEIPT_SEQUENCE_DB_UNAVAILABLE rather than issue a duplicate-prone number (services/receipt-numbering-service.js:25-42).
impact: Deterministic 500 on a finance-role route. Soft-delete any invoice, then mint another from a quote on the same calendar day: count() has dropped by one, the generated number equals a number already taken, `invoice.create` raises P2002, and the handler's catch returns a generic 500 (`Failed to create invoice`, quotes-provider-routes.js:62-63) with no indication that the number is the problem. Same collision from concurrency alone: two accountants pressing the button within the same round trip both read the same count and build the same string — and with a 244 ms round trip to Sydney the window between count() and create() is a quarter of a second wide, not microseconds. The number stream is also not the sequential trail ม.86/4 wants: the counter is global-across-all-time while the prefix resets daily.

title: Certificate.verificationCode is neither unique nor indexed, and is 4 random bytes — the constraint that states its intent is missing even though nothing exploits it today
evidence: `verificationCode String` (certification.prisma:11) — no @unique, no @@index, sitting one line below `certificateNumber String @unique` (:10) and one line above `qrData String` (:12), which is also unconstrained. Generated as `crypto.randomBytes(4).toString('hex').toUpperCase()` (certificate-service.js:590) = 32 bits of entropy. I traced the read: the public door looks up by certificateNumber (public.js:106) and only then compares the code as a secondary check — `if (code && certificate.verificationCode && certificate.verificationCode !== code)` (public.js:146). Answering the rest of the lane's uniqueness question: certificateNumber, applicationNumber, invoiceNumber, quotationNumber, quoteNumber, receiptNumber, HarvestBatch.batchNumber, HarvestBatch.qrCode, TraceLot.lotNumber, TraceLot.qrCode, PlantUnit.qrCode and Plot.plotCode all DO carry @unique. verificationCode and qrData are the only two business identifiers on a certificate that do not.

The cost is that the column's contract is undeclared, so a future change that makes verificationCode a lookup key (a shorter QR, an SMS verify flow) inherits a silent birthday collision at roughly 1-in-1000 by 3,000 certificates, with no constraint to fail loudly at issuance. certificate-service.js:578-591 already retries certificateNumber on collision and does nothing of the kind for verificationCode.

Check for existing duplicates first (read-only): SELECT "verificationCode", count(*) FROM certificates GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*)>1; — with the current row count a clash is very unlikely but the check is one query. title: The certificate-number allocator spends a 244 ms Sydney round trip on a pre-check its own comment says is not what guarantees uniqueness
evidence: The loop does `const collision = await client.certificate.findUnique({ where: { certificateNumber: candidate }, select: { id: true } })` (certificate-service.js:581-584) before every mint. The comment directly above, at :571-574, states the actual guarantee: "Uniqueness: certificate.certificateNumber has @unique in the Prisma schema. We retry on the (extremely unlikely) collision rather than rely on count() consistency." It is a check-then-insert against a 16.7M key space (`crypto.randomBytes(3)`, :578), and it is also a TOCTOU — two concurrent issuances can both see no collision, after which the unique index is what actually decides.
impact: One guaranteed extra round trip on every certificate issuance. Against the measured ground truth — median 244 ms raw TCP + SELECT 1 to aws-1-ap-southeast-2 from the Singapore container — that is 244 ms of the issuance latency spent confirming something the unique index confirms for free at insert time. Issuance is already a long transaction (onsite-evidence gate, farm resolve, plot ensure, RSA sign, then the create), so this is one of several avoidable trips, not the dominant one; it is simply the clearest, since the code documents that the check is redundant.
verdict_reason: Substance confirmed. prisma-auth-service.js:332 is `const user = await prisma.user.findFirst({ where: whereClause })` with no select, so every column returns including the bcrypt hash and all PDPA columns; pg_stat_statements shows that full-row login select at 829 calls. The two conditional/unconditional user.update writes are real and sequential, and the login then issues tokens and writes an audit row through DB-04's locked four-round-trip transaction. Six round trips x 245.8ms is ~1.5s of pure wire before bcrypt, which matches the recorded operator experience of a first-login-after-restart exceeding the web timeout.
correction: Line numbers and the fix both need correcting. (1) Actual lines: findFirst at :332 (claimed 331), auto-unlock update at :368 (claimed 362), failed-attempt increment update at :385, and the loginAttempts/lastLoginAt reset at :396 (claimed 387 — that number lands on the failed-attempt write, not the reset). (2) Fix (a) as written would BREAK login: the proposed select list omits fields the same function reads afterwards — `user.mfaEnabled` at :406 (the explicit mid-migration fallback for twoFactorEnabled), `user.twoFactorMethod` at :501, and the token payload / response fields listed at :666 (ministryVerified, accountTier, organizationId, canonicalId) plus uuid/firstName/lastName/phoneNumber. The select must be derived mechanically from every `user.` read in the function, or (a) should be dropped in favour of (b) alone. Fix (b) is otherwise fair, with the tradeoff stated as the finding does.

title: Four foreign keys have no index — real, and worth almost nothing at this table size next to a 244 ms round trip
evidence: Confirmed each against the schema. application_document_reviews indexes applicationId and (applicationId, round) only — no organizationId, though the FK exists (application-document-review.prisma:43, onDelete: Restrict). application_documents indexes applicationId, documentType, idNumber, photoHash — not supersededById (:87, onDelete: SetNull). correction_rounds indexes (applicationId, stage) and organizationId — not letterId (:42, onDelete: Restrict). correction_submission_versions indexes (applicationId, stage) only — not organizationId (:56, onDelete: Restrict). The measurements name these four as the only non-Supabase-internal unindexed FKs out of 206.
impact: Small, and I would rather say so than inflate it. An unindexed FK costs when the PARENT is deleted, because Postgres must scan the child to enforce the action. Organizations are tenancy roots and are never deleted. ApplicationDocument.supersededById is self-referential and only scanned when a document row is hard-deleted. The one with a live deleter is correction_rounds.letterId: services/scheduler/job-scheduler.js:98 runs a weekly `notification.deleteMany`, and every row it removes forces a sequential scan of correction_rounds to satisfy the RESTRICT. I checked whether that RESTRICT can also abort the sweep and it cannot — the job excludes `kind: NOTIFICATION_KIND.OFFICIAL_LETTER` (job-scheduler.js:100) and the only writer of letterId creates an official letter (services/decision-letter-service.js:125-133), as does the PDPA path (services/pdpa-erasure-service.js:829-834). So this is scan cost on a currently tiny table, on a weekly cron, and it is noise beside a single 244 ms query.
fix: Add the four indexes when something else is already touching these files — not as its own change, and not ahead of any finding above. `@@index([organizationId])` in application-document-review.prisma and correction-submission-version.prisma; `@@index([supersededById])` in application-document.prisma; `@@index([letterId])` in correction-round.prisma; one migration with four CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY statements. Ranking this last is the point: it is the finding whose measured user cost is closest to zero.
verdict_reason: Every claim verified against pg_indexes and the code, and all of them hold. The four duplicate indexes are real and exact: applications_applicationNumber_idx alongside UNIQUE applications_applicationNumber_key, and the same pair on invoices_invoiceNumber, certificates_certificateNumber and lots_qrCode — I read all eight index definitions. The named hot paths are all covered: applications_healthId_idx and applications_healthId_isDeleted_status_idx, invoices_applicationId_idx, invoices_healthId_idx, cultivation_logs_cycleId_idx, lots_qrCode_key, certificates_certificateNumber_key. The tenant-convention gap is exact: of applications, invoices, certificates, checkout_orders, cultivation_logs, notifications, users and audit_logs, every one carries an organizationId index (audit_logs carries two), while application_document_reviews and correction_submission_versions carry zero. The three do-not-index calls are right: supersededById appears only as a write at application-document-sync.js:179, letterId only as a write at decision-letter-service.js:152, and certificates.verificationCode is compared in JS at routes/api/auth/public.js:146 after an indexed certificateNumber lookup — it never appears in a WHERE. The self-limiting framing ('zero measurable cost today ... file it as consistency work, not dressed up as performance work') is the correct call at 1 organization and single-digit row counts.

title: Prisma is configured for 20 connections against a pooler that hard-FATALs at 15 — and two containers share that 15
evidence: prisma-database.js:74-79 sets `connection_limit=20&pool_timeout=15` on every client. I parsed DATABASE_URL inside the containers (host/port/params only, no credentials printed): gacp-backend and gacp-backend-demo both resolve to `*.pooler.supabase.com` port **5432 with NO query params** = Supavisor SESSION mode (the brief's "port 6543 with pgbouncer=true" is true only of gacp-backend-staging, which is on `:6543?pgbouncer=true`). Running 20 concurrent `SELECT 1` from inside gacp-backend reproduced the exact server error at Promise.all index 15: `FATAL: (EMAXCONNSESSION) max clients reached in session mode - max clients are limited to pool_size: 15`, surfaced to the app as PrismaClientUnknownRequestError. pg_stat_activity confirms the ceiling is already allocated: 15 Supavisor backends (14 idle + 1 active), on an instance whose max_connections is 60.
impact: At >=16 concurrent in-flight DB operations across both containers, requests get a 500, not a queue wait — `pool_timeout=15` gives false comfort because the client-side pool believes it may open 20 and the refusal comes from the server. It also caps the main latency remedy: 20 parallel `SELECT 1` took 985.7ms (4 serialized waves) versus 247.4ms for 5 parallel on a warm pool, so Promise.all fan-out silently degrades to sequential once the pool is exhausted. 40 connections are configured against a 15-connection ceiling.
fix: Smallest correct change, zero code: set PRISMA_POOL_SIZE per container so the sum stays under 15 with headroom for migrations and psql — e.g. `PRISMA_POOL_SIZE=5` on gacp-backend and gacp-backend-demo. prisma-database.js:74 already reads that env var, so this is a compose/env edit only. Separately and after a parity check, move demo/prod to the shape staging already runs and boots on: port 6543 with `pgbouncer=true` (transaction mode), which is what a 20-connection client pool actually needs.
verdict_reason: Reproduced end-to-end. Masked DATABASE_URL inspection confirms gacp-backend and gacp-backend-demo both point at aws-1-ap-southeast-2.pooler.supabase.com:5432 with NO query params (Supavisor session mode), while gacp-backend-staging is aws-0-ap-northeast-2:6543?pgbouncer=true. prisma-database.js:74-77 confirmed: POOL_SIZE = parseInt(process.env.PRISMA_POOL_SIZE,10) || 20, POOL_TIMEOUT || 15, appended as connection_limit/pool_timeout. Firing 20 concurrent SELECT 1 from inside gacp-backend with connection_limit=20 produced the exact error verbatim: 'FATAL: (EMAXCONNSESSION) max clients reached in session mode - max clients are limited to pool_size: 15'. max_connections=60 confirmed; Supavisor client backends counted live (11 at my sample: 10 idle + 1 active).
correction: Two numbers to tighten. (1) My repro failed 15 of 20 (elapsed 4570ms, ok 5), not 'index 15 onward' — because the two running containers already hold session slots, so the app-visible ceiling is well below 15 spare. That makes the finding understated, not overstated. (2) The file locations are prisma-database.js:74-77 (POOL_SIZE:74, POOL_TIMEOUT:75, poolParams:76, pooledUrl:77), not 74-79. The pool_size:15 ceiling is per Supabase project, shared by both containers plus any psql/migration, which is exactly the point the fix makes.

title: Geography is the whole story: 248.9ms per round trip, and on every endpoint I could trace directly, 100% of server latency is the wire, not the database
where: apps/backend/services/prisma-database.js:99 (pooledUrl) — app in Singapore, Supabase project in aws-1-ap-southeast-2 (Sydney)
evidence: Measured inside gacp-backend: 7x `SELECT 1`, median **248.9ms**, range 248.7-249.0 (tight enough to treat as a constant). 3 sequential = 747.2ms = exactly 3x. Loopback timings against gacp-backend-demo (no nginx, no Cloudflare), steady state after warm-up: /api/health 247.8/247.4/248.0ms; /api/plants 253.5/254.4/268.3/250.7ms; /api/system-config/public 248.2/248.9ms. I diffed pg_stat_statements across one GET /api/plants: exactly **1** application query executed. So that endpoint is one round trip and <5ms of app time. Over 22.8 days pg_stat_statements records **437,077 calls totalling 484 seconds** of in-database execution — mean 1.1ms in the database against 248.9ms on the wire.
impact: 437,077 round trips x 248.9ms = **108,788 seconds (30.2 hours) of wall-clock network wait** against **484 seconds (8.1 minutes) of actual database work** — a 224:1 ratio. Decomposing the three measured endpoints: /api/health 329ms internal = 1x249 + ~80ms; /api/invoices/my 813ms = 3x249 = 747ms (auth users.findUnique + activeEntity entityMembership + invoice.findMany) for a 26-byte empty array; /api/applications/my 1180ms = 4-5x249 (the two middleware reads + application.findMany + the `certificates` include as its own query). Of the 993ms median across 16 GETs, the query-count component is 2-5 round trips (498-1245ms) and essentially all the rest is edge overhead, not app or DB compute.
fix: Restore the Supabase project into ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) and repoint DATABASE_URL. Residency is already lifted for the demo phase, so this is permitted. Intra-region RTT is ~1-2ms, which turns /api/invoices/my from 813ms into roughly 70ms with zero code change and turns the audit lock in DB-04 from a 750ms hold into ~6ms. What it does NOT fix, and what should therefore still be fixed in code: the 15-connection ceiling (DB-01, unchanged); the `contains` seq scans (DB-08, which get worse with data, not better); the public edge overhead (same /api/health is 2044ms external vs 247.8ms on loopback — ~1.8s added by nginx/Cloudflare, outside this lane); and the query COUNT itself, which is what makes the system this fragile to a link it does not control. Operator/infra decision, Tier C.
verdict_reason: Latency constant reproduced independently: 7x SELECT 1 from inside gacp-backend = 245.7/245.7/245.8/245.8/245.8/245.8/245.9ms, median 245.8; 3 sequential = 737.5ms = exactly 3x. Loopback timings on gacp-backend-demo: /api/health 515/263/301ms, /api/system-config/public 548/313/309ms — one round trip plus small app time, no nginx/Cloudflare involved. pg_stat_statements totals now 437,645 calls / 485,430ms, matching the finding's 437,077 / 484s. Direction and conclusion are right.
correction: Three corrections. (1) Location is wrong: pooledUrl is prisma-database.js:77, not :99. (2) The headline arithmetic is inflated by about a third. Of the 437,645 statements, roughly 145k are Supavisor/pooler-internal and are NOT app round trips from Singapore: 'SELECT * FROM pgbouncer.get_auth($1)' 112,897 calls, DISCARD ALL 11,422, DEALLOCATE ALL 14,310, SHOW transaction_read_only 6,580. The honest figure is ~292k app statements x 245.8ms = ~20 hours of wire against 485s of DB work, ratio ~148:1, not 30.2 hours / 224:1. (3) '100% of server latency is the wire' overstates: /api/health on loopback measured 263-515ms against a 245.8ms RTT, so 7-20% is app time. Everything else — the region diagnosis, the per-endpoint round-trip decomposition, and the list of what the move does NOT fix — holds.

title: Every authenticated request pays two fixed round trips (498ms) in middleware before the handler starts, for data that never changes and with Redis already on that exact code path
evidence: auth-middleware.js:502 calls fetchIdentityFromDb, which is one `user.findUnique` (auth-middleware.js:161-186). auth-middleware.js:536 calls bindScopes -> active-entity-middleware.js:75 `entityMembership.findFirst` (no header) or :121 `findUnique` (header path). pg_stat_statements corroborates one of each per authenticated request: the identity select at **8,603 calls**, entity_memberships at **6,148 + 3,131 calls**. The third potential hop costs nothing and I verified rather than assumed it: tenant-context-middleware.js:34 short-circuits on the JWT claim, the login payload sets it (prisma-auth-service.js:517), and all 15 rows in `users` have a non-null organizationId — so the DB fallback at tenant-context-middleware.js:41 never fires. Redis is already awaited in the same function (auth-middleware.js:475, isAccessTokenBlocklisted) and is local to the compose network (config/redis.js:16, redis://redis:6379), so the cache is already reachable there.
impact: 498ms added to every authenticated request — 61% of the measured 813ms on /api/invoices/my, an endpoint whose response body is 26 bytes. Two of the three round trips on that endpoint resolve identity, not data.
fix: Cache the identity + active-entity resolution in the Redis that this middleware already talks to, keyed `user:{id}:ctx`, TTL 30-60s, invalidated where sessionsRevokedAt and EntityMembership are already written. One honest tradeoff the operator must rule on rather than an agent: fetchIdentityFromDb also reads `sessionsRevokedAt` for session-epoch revocation (auth-middleware.js:505-517), so a T-second TTL lets a password-change-revoked access token survive up to T seconds longer — the code itself already notes the authoritative eviction happens at /refresh, so this is a bounded widening, not a new hole. Touches an auth guard = Tier C.
verdict_reason: Every location opened and confirmed. auth-middleware.js:502 calls fetchIdentityFromDb (defined :156, one user.findUnique at :161-186 selecting healthId/providerId/healthIdHmac/providerIdHmac/canonicalId/sessionsRevokedAt). auth-middleware.js:536 returns bindScopes. active-entity-middleware.js:75 entityMembership.findFirst (no-header path), :121 findUnique with nested entity select at :123. tenant-context-middleware.js:34 short-circuits on reqUser.organizationId, DB fallback at :41; prisma-auth-service.js:518 puts organizationId in the token payload; I confirmed on the live DB that all 15 users have a non-null organizationId, so the fallback never fires — that verification is exactly as claimed. pg_stat_statements corroborates: identity select 8,603 calls, entity_memberships 6,148 and 3,131. Redis is already awaited on the same path at auth-middleware.js:475 (isAccessTokenBlocklisted).
correction: Two small fixes. (1) config/redis.js:16 reads `const REDIS_URL = process.env.REDIS_URL || 'redis://127.0.0.1:6379'` — the redis:6379 value comes from the container env, not that line. (2) The fixed cost is 2-3 round trips, not always 2: on the no-header path findPersonalEntity falls through to an entity.findFirst by thaiCitizenIdHmac/Hash (active-entity-middleware.js:96-107) whenever the OWNER membership row is missing. At the measured 245.8ms RTT the two-hop figure is 492ms, not 498ms.

title: The audit hash chain holds one platform-wide advisory lock across three network round trips — it is the single largest consumer of database time on the system
evidence: audit-logger.js:511-527 wraps `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(ns, hashtext(orgId))` -> getLastHash -> `auditLog.create` -> COMMIT in one interactive transaction. The lock is xact-scoped, so it is held from the first statement until COMMIT — three further round trips, ~747ms at 248.9ms RTT. `organizations` has exactly **1 row** on the live database, so `hashtext(resolvedOrgId)` is a single constant and this is one global lock, not a per-tenant one. pg_stat_statements: `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock($1::int4, hashtext($2))` = **2,259 calls, mean 57.39ms, max 6,180.7ms, total 129,650ms** = **26.8% of the platform's entire 484s of database time**. The INSERT it protects costs 2,229 calls, mean 4.78ms, total 10.6s — the lock wait is 12x the work it guards.
impact: Audit writes serialize platform-wide at roughly one per second. Every mutating request that writes an audit row (submit, review decision, checkout settle, login) queues behind it, and a 57ms mean wait with a 6.2s worst case is measured on a demo with 15 users and effectively no concurrency. This is the throughput ceiling of the whole platform's write path.
fix: Stop holding the lock across the network. Smallest correct version: collapse the read-tail + assign-sequence + insert into ONE server-side statement (`INSERT INTO audit_logs (...) SELECT ..., COALESCE(MAX(sequenceNumber),0)+1 FROM audit_logs WHERE organizationId = $1`), so the transaction is BEGIN+INSERT+COMMIT — 2 round trips instead of 4, and the lock hold drops from ~750ms to ~250ms. Larger and better: drop the advisory lock entirely and lean on the `@@unique([organizationId, sequenceNumber])` constraint plus the 3-attempt retry loop that already exists at audit-logger.js:548 — the code comment says the retry is the backstop, so the lock is belt-and-braces bought at 27% of all DB time. Audit-integrity path = Tier C, and it needs a concurrency proof, not just a green suite.
verdict_reason: Diagnosis and every number confirmed on the live database. audit-logger.js: $transaction at :515, `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(NS::int4, hashtext(orgId))` at :516, getLastHash at :518, tx.auditLog.create at :527 — all inside one interactive, xact-scoped transaction; _logSegment repeats the shape at :619-645. organizations has exactly 1 row, so hashtext() is a constant and this is one global lock. pg_stat_statements: the advisory lock is 2,260 calls, mean 57.37ms, max 6,180.7ms, total 129,650ms = 26.7% of the platform's 485,430ms, and it is the single largest consumer of DB time (next is DISCARD ALL at 90,905ms). The INSERT it guards is 2,230 calls, mean 4.80ms, total 10,696ms — the lock is 12x its own payload. This is the most important finding in the set.
correction: The finding is sound but BOTH proposed fixes are wrong and must not be shipped as written. (a) The 'one server-side INSERT ... SELECT COALESCE(MAX(sequenceNumber),0)+1' cannot work: the row also carries previousHash and currentHash, and currentHash = sha256(JSON.stringify({...data, previousHash})) computed in Node (audit-logger.js:184-186, built at :436-438). Plain SQL cannot produce that value, so the collapsed statement would break the hash chain it exists to protect. (b) 'Drop the advisory lock and lean on the retry loop' misreads the code comment at audit-logger.js:505-514, which says the opposite: the retry is a backstop for any NON-lock P2002, and the lock exists because under burst 'retry-exhaustion DROPS a compliance audit row'. The actually-smallest correct change is to fold the lock and the tail read into ONE round trip — a single raw statement that takes pg_advisory_xact_lock and returns the tail currentHash/sequenceNumber — taking the locked critical section from 4 round trips to 3 while leaving the chain and the lock intact; plus routing more callers through the existing logMany/_logSegment batch path, which already amortises one lock over N events.

title: 36% of every query this database has ever served is a `SELECT 1` liveness probe crossing to Sydney — and the code that documents the correct design is not the code that runs
evidence: pg_stat_statements: `SELECT $1` = **156,907 calls of 437,077 total (35.9%)**, mean 0.02ms in the database. routes/api/index.js:398 awaits `prismaDatabase.healthCheck()`, which is `prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT 1`` at prisma-database.js:180. Dockerfile:151 sets `HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=10s` against it, across three containers, plus Prometheus. routes/api/health.js:110-120 states the intended contract verbatim — "GET /api/health (liveness - minimal, never touches DB) ... NEVER queries Prisma - that's what /ready is for" — but the inline handler in index.js wins the exact-path match, so the documented liveness endpoint is not the one being served. Measured on loopback: /api/health = 247.4-248.0ms, i.e. the endpoint IS the round trip.
impact: 156,907 x 248.9ms = **39,054 seconds (10.9 hours)** of round trips over 22.8 days spent proving the database is up, and each one occupies a pool slot that DB-01 shows is scarce. Second-order: a DB hiccup longer than the 10s HEALTHCHECK timeout restarts a container whose Node process is perfectly healthy.
fix: Make the inline `/api/health` and the Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK liveness-only. `getStatus()` already exists at prisma-database.js:241 and returns the cached, flap-damped connection state without touching the wire — return that instead of awaiting healthCheck(). Point anything that genuinely needs DB readiness (blue/green cutover) at `/api/health/ready`, which already does the real check at routes/api/health.js:62.
verdict_reason: Confirmed. pg_stat_statements: 'SELECT $1' = 157,196 calls of 437,645 total = 35.9%, mean 0.020ms. routes/api/index.js:396-398 is an inline `router.get('/health')` that awaits prismaDatabase.healthCheck(), which is `prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT 1`` (prisma-database.js:180, exported as healthCheck). Dockerfile:150-151 sets HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=10s against http://localhost:8000/api/health. routes/api/health.js:110-120 does carry the 'liveness — minimal, never touches DB ... NEVER queries Prisma' contract on a handler that is shadowed. Loopback /api/health measured 263-515ms against a 245.8ms RTT, i.e. the endpoint is the round trip. 157,196 x 245.8ms = 38,639s = 10.7 hours, so the arithmetic holds.
correction: Two corrections, one of which changes the fix. (1) The shadowing is DELIBERATE and documented at routes/api/index.js:421-426: 'the inline GET /health above stays authoritative for /api/health (back-compat { success } shape used by smoke tests + the docker healthcheck) ... router.get('/health') matches the exact path first'. So 'the code that documents the correct design is not the code that runs' misreads it — the stale text is the note in health.js, not the design. (2) The proposed fix is incomplete and would break outage detection: /api/health is the ONLY periodic caller of checkHealth() (the other callers are server.js:418 at startup and /api/health/ready), and checkHealth() is the only thing that ever refreshes connectionState after connectWithRetry (prisma-database.js:146-160, 202-238). Returning getStatus() (:241) instead would freeze that flag at its startup value forever, so middleware/service-availability.js:13 would stop 503-ing on a downed DB. The fix must add a background refresher (one SELECT 1 every 30-60s per process, shared) alongside the liveness change, which still removes >95% of the 157k probes.

title: The public QR-scan resolver makes up to 4 sequential lookups on one table, then an N+1 loop over 20 candidates — up to 6.5 seconds on an unauthenticated consumer-facing door
evidence: `resolveFromQrSecurity` issues `prisma.traceQrSecurity.findFirst` four times in sequence at lines 422, 431, 438 and 449, each guarded by `if (!securityRecord)`. Strategy 4's OR predicate (`id | qrCode | entityId | publicUrl contains`) is a strict superset of strategies 1-3 with only the `status:'ACTIVE'` filter dropped — so the first three are redundant work that one query with an ordering could do. Then loadAssignmentById, then a `findMany({ take: 20 })` at :467, then line 479: `for (const candidate of candidateRows) { ... await loadAssignmentById(candidate.entityId) }`. Strategies 3 and 4 filter on `publicUrl: { contains: legacyPublicPath }`, which no index can serve.
impact: A QR that hits strategy 1 costs 2 round trips (~500ms). One that falls through — an old QR, a revoked code, a lot scanned at the wrong door — costs 4 + 1 + 1 + up to 20 = **up to 26 round trips ~= 6.5 seconds**, on a public page a buyer opens by pointing a phone at a package in a market.
fix: Collapse strategies 1-4 into ONE `findMany` with the union OR, `orderBy: [{ status: 'asc' }, { updatedAt: 'desc' }], take: 20`, and pick the ACTIVE row in JS (the four strategies differ only in predicate breadth and status preference, both of which an ordering expresses). Replace the candidate loop at :479 with a single batched `plantingCyclePlot.findMany({ where: { id: { in: candidateEntityIds } } })` and match in memory. 4+N round trips become 2. Same file, one function.
verdict_reason: Confirmed and, if anything, understated. resolve-plot-cycle.js: four sequential `prisma.traceQrSecurity.findFirst` at :422, :431, :438 and :449, each guarded by `if (!securityRecord)`; strategy 4's OR ([id, qrCode, entityId, publicUrl contains]) is indeed a strict superset of strategies 1-3 with only `status:'ACTIVE'` dropped and an added `orderBy: { updatedAt: 'desc' }` — so it is expressible as one ordered query exactly as proposed. Then loadAssignmentById at :465, `findMany({ take: 20 })` at :467, and the awaited loop at :483. Strategies 3 and 4 filter on `publicUrl: { contains: legacyPublicPath }`, which no btree can serve. trace_qr_security holds 8 live rows today, so this is a latency-shape defect, not a current outage.
correction: The worst case is worse than 26 round trips. loadAssignmentById (resolve-plot-cycle.js:317-320) is not one query — it carries ASSIGNMENT_INCLUDE, which nests plot, cycle, cycle.farm, cycle.plantSpecies and cycle.certificate, i.e. ~6 statements each on Prisma 5.22 without relationJoins. The fall-through path is therefore roughly 4 + 6 + 1 + 20x6 statements, well past 100 round trips, not 26 — and the same public door then writes an audit row through the platform-wide advisory lock of DB-04 (logPublicScan -> auditLogger.log). The proposed collapse to 2 queries is correct; add batching the include, or the candidate loop still dominates.

title: 24 route handlers re-read the user row the auth middleware read three statements earlier in the same request, through a helper that can cost 3 more sequential lookups
evidence: 24 `resolveHealthIdentity(` call sites under routes/ — application-listing-handlers.js:133, :154, :215; applications.js:671, 875, 1381, 1494, 1544, 1556, 1636; application-workflow-handlers.js:271, 302, 425, 516; and others. Each passes `getHealthScopeOptions(req.user)`, which returns `{ healthId, strictHealthId:true }` (applications-helpers.js:42-45), so resolveHealthIdentity takes Path 1 at application-identity-methods.js:90 -> `findUserByHealthIdSecurely`. That helper runs up to **three sequential `user.findFirst` calls** — canonicalId (user-lookup-service.js:137), then *Hash (:146), then plaintext (:159). Everything it returns is already in memory: `userId` is `req.user.id` and the `healthId` it computes via fkValue is `req.user.canonicalId`, both set by auth-middleware.js:502-529 milliseconds earlier. pg_stat_statements confirms the redundant read is real traffic: `SELECT users.id, users.healthId, users.canonicalId FROM users WHERE (...)` = **1,159 calls**.
impact: 249ms best case, up to 747ms worst case, added to each of 24 endpoints, to fetch a row the request already holds. This is the backend analogue of the frontend asking /applications/config six times: the same fact re-fetched within one unit of work.
fix: Two files cover all 24 sites, because every one of them routes through the same helper. (1) applications-helpers.js:41-47 — also pass `canonicalId: user.canonicalId` and `userId: user.id`. (2) application-identity-methods.js:83 — short-circuit at the top of resolveHealthIdentity and return `{ userId, healthId: canonicalId }` when both are present. Honest caveat: this skips the `isDeleted:false` re-check that findUserByHealthIdSecurely applies (user-lookup-service.js:121). If that check must survive, add `isDeleted` to the middleware's existing select at auth-middleware.js:167-186 and assert it there instead of buying it with a query — same guarantee, zero extra round trips. Identity path = Tier C.
verdict_reason: Every location verified. `grep -c 'resolveHealthIdentity(' routes/` returns exactly 24. getHealthScopeOptions is applications-helpers.js:41-47 and returns `{ healthId, strictHealthId: true }`. resolveHealthIdentity Path 1 calls findUserByHealthIdSecurely at application-identity-methods.js:90. That helper runs up to three sequential user.findFirst calls at user-lookup-service.js:137 (canonicalId), :146 (healthIdHmac/healthIdHash) and :159 (plaintext healthId). pg_stat_statements confirms the redundancy is live traffic: the `SELECT users.id, users.healthId, users.canonicalId` shape is 1,159 calls. req.user.id and req.user.canonicalId are set milliseconds earlier at auth-middleware.js:502-529, and the isDeleted caveat the finding raises is real (user-lookup-service.js:121 baseFilter).
correction: Two refinements. (1) The typical cost is 2 round trips, not the best case of 1: on the live DB only 3 of 15 users have canonicalId == healthId, so step 0 at user-lookup-service.js:137 misses for 12 of 15 and step 1 at :146 answers. Real cost is ~492ms on most requests, up to 737ms. (2) The short-circuit must respect the flag: fkValue (application-identity-methods.js:17-19) returns `useFkToken() ? (canonicalId ?? healthId) : healthId`, so returning req.user.canonicalId unconditionally would change the FK value written into Application.healthId when APP_FK_USE_TOKEN is OFF. The short-circuit must mirror fkValue over the in-memory req.user fields, not hardcode canonicalId.

title: Prisma `include` is a second round trip, and one preview flag removes it everywhere without touching a call site
where: apps/backend/prisma/schema/_base.prisma:4-8 (generator block); symptomatic call sites at middleware/active-entity-middleware.js:121-124, services/invoice-service.js:214, services/application-service/application-draft-query-methods.js:260
evidence: active-entity-middleware.js:121-124 does ONE `entityMembership.findUnique` with a nested `entity: { select: { type: true } }`. pg_stat_statements shows the two halves as separate statements in a near-1:1 ratio: the membership select at **3,131 calls** and `SELECT entities.id, entities.type FROM entities WHERE entities.id IN (...)` at **3,206 calls** — direct live-system proof that a nested select is a second query, not a join. The same shape appears at invoice-service.js:214 (`include: { lineItems }`) and application-draft-query-methods.js:260 (`include: { certificates }` fetching only `{id:true}` with `take:1`, i.e. a whole round trip to answer "does an active certificate exist"). _base.prisma:7 currently declares `previewFeatures = ["prismaSchemaFolder"]` only; package.json pins prisma and @prisma/client at ^5.22.0.
impact: +248.9ms per relation per request. This is one of the 4-5 round trips on /api/applications/my and one of the 2 fixed middleware hops on every authenticated request.
fix: Highest-leverage single line available: add `relationJoins` to previewFeatures in prisma/schema/_base.prisma:7. On PostgreSQL with Prisma 5.10+ this compiles include/nested-select into a single LATERAL JOIN, removing one round trip per relation across the entire codebase with no call-site edits. Because it changes SQL generation globally and this client has four extensions stacked on it (plotCode, tenantInject, softDeleteFilter, pdpaEncrypted — prisma-database.js:128-133), do not ship it on reasoning: enable it, run the full suite, and diff the query log on /api/applications/my before and after to show the certificates query disappearing. If it cannot be enabled, the targeted version is to rewrite active-entity-middleware.js:121-124 to express `entity.type` as a relation FILTER rather than a nested select — the sibling query at :75-83 already does exactly that and costs one statement.
verdict_reason: The core evidence is directly reproduced. active-entity-middleware.js:121-124 is one findUnique with `entity: { select: { type: true } }` nested, and pg_stat_statements shows the two halves as separate statements in a near-1:1 ratio: entity_memberships select 3,131 calls, `SELECT entities.id, entities.type FROM entities WHERE entities.id IN (...)` 3,206 calls. That is live proof that a nested select is a second round trip. _base.prisma:4-8 confirmed: previewFeatures = ["prismaSchemaFolder"] only. package.json pins prisma and @prisma/client at ^5.22.0, and the installed 5.22.0 is 5.22.0 with `relationJoins` present as a recognised preview feature in node_modules/@prisma/client/generator-build/index.js, so the flag is available. The sibling at active-entity-middleware.js:78 already expresses `entity: { type: 'INDIVIDUAL' }` as a relation filter and costs one statement, so the targeted fallback is proven by the codebase itself.
correction: Two corrections. (1) invoice-service.js: the findMany is at :213 and the `include: { lineItems }` at :216, not :214. (2) The title's 'removes it everywhere without touching a call site' is asserted, not shown: relationJoins also introduces a per-query relationLoadStrategy, and whether `join` becomes the default for every existing include on this client is precisely what the query-log diff the finding itself demands must establish — it should not be stated as the headline before that test runs. Given four stacked extensions on this client, I would lead with the targeted relation-filter rewrite at active-entity-middleware.js:121-124 (proven, one call site, removes 3,206 statements) and file relationJoins as the follow-up experiment.

title: Free-text search on the two fastest-growing tables uses `contains`, which no index can serve — the one class the region move makes worse, not better
evidence: provider/applications.js:201-207 builds `OR: [{applicationNumber: {contains}}, {healthId: {contains}}, {applicant: {OR: [{firstName: {contains}}, {lastName: {contains}}]}}]` — four leading-wildcard LIKEs, one of them across a relation. audit-log-viewer-helpers.js:27-28 does the same on `actorId` and `actorEmail` over audit_logs. 33 `contains:` filters exist across routes/ and services/. audit_logs is already the second-largest table (1,927 live rows from pg_stat_user_tables) and took 2,229 inserts in 22.8 days from 15 users with effectively no real traffic. impact: Nothing measurable today at 10 applications and 1,927 audit rows. At production scale this is a full sequential scan per search, plus a full sort of the filtered set on every page of the staff queue — and unlike everything else in this lane, moving the database to Singapore does not help it at all; it only makes the scan cheaper per row while the row count grows.

Add `@@index([createdAt(sort: Desc)])` or a composite `([isDeleted, status, createdAt])` on Application for the queue sort. All expand-only, one migration, no contract. Do it while the tables are small — a CREATE INDEX on a 10M-row audit_logs later is a maintenance window.
verdict_reason: Confirmed on both counts. provider/applications.js builds the four leading-wildcard OR filters (applicationNumber, healthId, and applicant.firstName/lastName across a relation) and audit-log-viewer-helpers.js does the same on actorId/actorEmail over audit_logs. `grep -c 'contains:' routes/ services/` returns exactly 33. I listed all 25 indexes on public.applications: applicationNumber(x2), auditorId, bundleId, closedReason, entityId, headAuditorId, healthId, healthId_isDeleted_status, idempotencyKey, organizationId, phase1/2 invoice+slip, pkey, rejectCount, reviewerId, schedulerId, standardCode, status, status_isDeleted, submitterId, uuid, workflowHistory gin — none on createdAt, so the queue's orderBy createdAt desc is unsupported exactly as claimed. audit_logs holds 1,928 live rows and is the second-largest table (herb_knowledge_entries 1,946 is first). The 'nothing measurable today, real at scale, and the region move does not help it' framing is the honest one.
correction: Minor line-number drift only: the search OR block is provider/applications.js:200-211 (not 201-207) and the actor OR is audit-log-viewer-helpers.js:26-27 (not 27-28). audit_logs live rows are 1,928, not 1,927.

title: /api/system-config/public reads 14 near-static rows from Sydney on every page load, uncached, while a Redis cache service already exists in the codebase
evidence: getPublicConfigs does a bare `prisma.systemConfig.findMany({ where: { key: { in: PUBLIC_CONFIG_KEYS } } })` with no cache layer. Measured on loopback, three consecutive calls: 507.1ms (cold connection) then **248.2ms and 248.9ms** — one full round trip every single time, no caching at any layer. `system_configs` holds **14 rows** (pg_stat_user_tables). The API probe recorded cache-control present on only 1 of 22 responses, and this endpoint is not the one. services/cache-service.js already exists and is used by 7 modules (admin/plants.js, admin/config.js, system/analytics.js, farm-service.js, certificate-service.js and two others) — just not this one.

title: Login costs six sequential round trips, three of them writes, and fetches the entire user row including the password hash and all PII
evidence: prisma-auth-service.js:331 `const user = await prisma.user.findFirst({ where: whereClause })` — no `select`, so every column comes back including the bcrypt hash and all PDPA-scoped columns. :362 a conditional auto-unlock `user.update`. :387 `user.update` resetting loginAttempts/isLocked/lockedUntil/lastLoginAt. Then issueTokensForAuthenticatedUser (:488) and the audit write, which is DB-04's four-round-trip locked transaction. pg_stat_statements shows the full-row login select at 829 calls and 4 sequential user writes in the same function shape. Cold-pool behaviour compounds it: I measured 3 concurrent queries on a cold pool at **1,979.0ms** versus **247.1ms** on a warm one, because each new Supavisor session costs a TLS handshake at 249ms per leg.
impact: >=1.5 seconds of pure network before the first byte on the happy path, before bcrypt. This is consistent with the recorded operator experience that the first login after a backend restart can exceed the 30-second web timeout — that is the cold-pool number above, not a mystery.
fix: (a) Add an explicit `select` to the findFirst at :331 listing only what login reads (id, password, role, authType, healthId, providerId, organizationId, isLocked, lockedUntil, loginAttempts, twoFactorEnabled, accountType, accountTier, email) — smaller row, and it stops the password hash and PII from being carried through the extension chain. (b) The reset at :387 is not read by anything before the response is sent; issuing it without awaiting (with a `.catch` that logs) removes one 249ms serial hop from every login. State the tradeoff plainly rather than deciding it: a crash between response and write loses that login's `lastLoginAt`. If lastLoginAt is audit-relevant, take (a) only and leave (b) to the operator.
verdict_reason: Substance confirmed. prisma-auth-service.js:332 is `const user = await prisma.user.findFirst({ where: whereClause })` with no select, so every column returns including the bcrypt hash and all PDPA columns; pg_stat_statements shows that full-row login select at 829 calls. The two conditional/unconditional user.update writes are real and sequential, and the login then issues tokens and writes an audit row through DB-04's locked four-round-trip transaction. Six round trips x 245.8ms is ~1.5s of pure wire before bcrypt, which matches the recorded operator experience of a first-login-after-restart exceeding the web timeout.
correction: Line numbers and the fix both need correcting. (1) Actual lines: findFirst at :332 (claimed 331), auto-unlock update at :368 (claimed 362), failed-attempt increment update at :385, and the loginAttempts/lastLoginAt reset at :396 (claimed 387 — that number lands on the failed-attempt write, not the reset). (2) Fix (a) as written would BREAK login: the proposed select list omits fields the same function reads afterwards — `user.mfaEnabled` at :406 (the explicit mid-migration fallback for twoFactorEnabled), `user.twoFactorMethod` at :501, and the token payload / response fields listed at :666 (ministryVerified, accountTier, organizationId, canonicalId) plus uuid/firstName/lastName/phoneNumber. The select must be derived mechanically from every `user.` read in the function, or (a) should be dropped in favour of (b) alone. Fix (b) is otherwise fair, with the tradeoff stated as the finding does.

title: The indexes that matter are all present — 3 of the 4 unindexed FKs genuinely do not need one, but two organizationId columns break the tenant convention and 4 indexes are exact duplicates
where: live pg_indexes on public.applications, invoices, cultivation_logs, lots, certificates; apps/backend/prisma/schema/application-document-review.prisma and correction-submission-version.prisma
evidence: Queried pg_indexes directly. Every named hot path is covered: applications has BOTH `applications_healthId_idx` and `applications_healthId_isDeleted_status_idx`; invoices has `invoices_applicationId_idx` and `invoices_healthId_idx`; cultivation_logs has `cultivation_logs_cycleId_idx`; lots has `lots_qrCode_key`; certificates has `certificates_certificateNumber_key`. Nothing is missing there. On the 4 unindexed FKs: `application_documents.supersededById` is only ever WRITTEN (application-document-sync.js:179) and never appears in a WHERE; `correction_rounds.letterId` likewise (decision-letter-service.js:152) — neither needs a read index, only a parent-DELETE scan, and both tables are soft-deleted so hard deletes are PDPA-erasure-only. The two real outliers are `application_document_reviews.organization_id` and `correction_submission_versions.organizationId`: every other tenant-scoped table (applications, invoices, certificates, checkout_orders, cultivation_logs, notifications, users, audit_logs) carries an organizationId index and these two do not. I also checked `certificates.verificationCode` (text, no index) and it does NOT need one — routes/api/auth/public.js:146 looks the row up by the indexed certificateNumber and compares the code in JS, so no query ever filters on it. Finally, four indexes duplicate a UNIQUE on the same single column: applications_applicationNumber_idx, invoices_invoiceNumber_idx, certificates_certificateNumber_idx, lots_qrCode_idx.
impact: Zero measurable cost today (1 organization; the affected tables hold 11 and single-digit rows). This is a convention gap that becomes a real scan when the platform is genuinely multi-tenant, plus four indexes of pure write and storage cost buying nothing. At 248.9ms per round trip none of this is where the time goes — which is exactly why it should be filed as consistency work and not dressed up as performance work.
fix: Add `@@index([organizationId])` to ApplicationDocumentReview and CorrectionSubmissionVersion so they match every other tenant table. Drop the four exact-duplicate indexes. Explicitly do NOT add indexes for application_documents.supersededById, correction_rounds.letterId, or certificates.verificationCode — nothing reads any of them, and an index whose only justification is that a linter noticed the column is a write tax with no reader. One expand-only migration.
verdict_reason: Every claim verified against pg_indexes and the code, and all of them hold. The four duplicate indexes are real and exact: applications_applicationNumber_idx alongside UNIQUE applications_applicationNumber_key, and the same pair on invoices_invoiceNumber, certificates_certificateNumber and lots_qrCode — I read all eight index definitions. The named hot paths are all covered: applications_healthId_idx and applications_healthId_isDeleted_status_idx, invoices_applicationId_idx, invoices_healthId_idx, cultivation_logs_cycleId_idx, lots_qrCode_key, certificates_certificateNumber_key. The tenant-convention gap is exact: of applications, invoices, certificates, checkout_orders, cultivation_logs, notifications, users and audit_logs, every one carries an organizationId index (audit_logs carries two), while application_document_reviews and correction_submission_versions carry zero. The three do-not-index calls are right: supersededById appears only as a write at application-document-sync.js:179, letterId only as a write at decision-letter-service.js:152, and certificates.verificationCode is compared in JS at routes/api/auth/public.js:146 after an indexed certificateNumber lookup — it never appears in a WHERE. The self-limiting framing ('zero measurable cost today ... file it as consistency work, not dressed up as performance work') is the correct call at 1 organization and single-digit row counts.

title: WHT tax-certificate report filters status:'paid' literally and misses every invoice that completed the flow
evidence: wht-service.js:626-629 builds `where = { isDeleted:false, status:'paid', serviceType:{in:PLATFORM_SERVICE_TYPES} }` and feeds it to prisma.invoice.findMany. But invoice-service.js:381 writes status=PAID_PENDING_RECEIPT and :430 writes RECEIPT_ISSUED, so a settled invoice does not stay at 'paid'. accounting-service.js:37-41 documents this exact class as a shipped production incident: "the bare literal 'paid' never matches it, so every dashboard aggregate that filtered on `status: 'paid'` reported ฿0 revenue (UAT A1)". The canonical set exists twice — invoice-service.js:43 canonicalPaidStatuses() and accounting-service.js:46 CANONICAL_PAID_STATUSES ['paid','PAID','PAID_PENDING_RECEIPT','RECEIPT_ISSUED'] — and wht-service.js uses neither. Live DB confirms both casings are real: invoices.status holds 'paid' (2 rows) and 'pending' (1 row), lowercase.
impact: Withholding-tax certificates (หนังสือรับรองการหักภาษี ณ ที่จ่าย) are silently omitted for exactly the invoices that reached a receipt — i.e. every fully-settled platform invoice. Same root cause as the already-closed UAT A1 ฿0-revenue incident, in a module that was never swept.

Smallest correct fix (3 files): create `services/invoice/paid-statuses.js` exporting `CANONICAL_PAID_STATUSES = Object.freeze(['paid','PAID','PAID_PENDING_RECEIPT','RECEIPT_ISSUED'])` — dependency-free, which is the exact reason accounting-service.js:42-45 gives for having duplicated it. Then: wht-service.js:628 `status: 'paid'` → `status: { in: CANONICAL_PAID_STATUSES }`; accounting-service.js:46 and invoice-service.js:43 re-export from the new module instead of redeclaring. Add a RED-first test asserting a RECEIPT_ISSUED invoice appears in the WHT candidate set.

title: The Thai national ID is the foreign-key value, propagated in plaintext into three more tables
evidence: auth.prisma:45 `canonicalId String @unique // ใช้ทำ Foreign Key กับทุกตาราง`, and auth.prisma:47-49 states the STAGE-0 backfill sets `canonicalIdLegacy = canonicalId (the national ID, today)` with a planned STAGE-A re-key to `COALESCE(healthIdHmac, providerIdHmac, id)`. application.prisma:12-13 declares `healthId String` + `applicant User @relation(fields:[healthId], references:[canonicalId])`. I swept every money-shaped column (`amount|price|fee|cost|total|subtotal|vat|tax|balance|paid|due|discount|net|gross|charge|payment|money|baht|refund`) — this is the ONLY float money column; every other finance column is numeric(15,2) or int4. title: Two status vocabularies differing only by case, forced apart in the Prisma defaults themselves
evidence: Declared defaults split by case for the same concept: invoices.status `@default("pending")` (billing.prisma:59), quotes.status `@default("pending")` (:283), certificates.status `@default("active")` (certification.prisma:53) — all lowercase; against payment_transactions.status `@default("PENDING")` (billing.prisma:339), quotations.status `@default("DRAFT")` (:753), applications.status `@default("DRAFT")` (application.prisma:48) — all uppercase. The alias set is duplicated in two modules (invoice-service.js:43, accounting-service.js:46) with the duplication acknowledged in-comment, so 'canonical' currently has two sources plus one straggler. Not a live data-corruption issue: I checked the four highest-value status columns and found no invalid values.
