Smallest correct step: land the shared `paid-statuses.js` from SCH-01 first so there is ONE source, then normalise forward only — change the Prisma defaults at billing.prisma:59,283 and certification.prisma:53 to uppercase, add a data migration UPDATE for the ~6 affected rows, and delete RAW_STATUS_ALIAS/statusFilterForQuery once green. Tier C (money + schema). Propose only.

title: 236 enum-shaped text columns, only 13 guarded by a CHECK — and the 20-state workflow column is not one of them
evidence: Zero Postgres ENUM types exist, and zero `enum` blocks are declared anywhere in prisma/schema/*.prisma (`grep -rn '^enum '` returns nothing across all 33 files, 6498 lines) — so the measurement's '0 enum types' is a declaration fact, not a mapping artefact. Of 1136 text columns, 236 are semantically enums by name (status/state/role/type/kind/method/stage/verdict/etc). `status` alone is a text column in 42 tables. The team's actual substitute is text + CHECK, and it works: 30 CHECK constraints exist, 13 of them value-list guards on exactly the newest tables — checkout_orders.status/milestone/dtam_remittance_status, correction_rounds.stage, application_document_reviews.verdict, dtam_remittance_batches.status, notifications.kind, identity_links.provider, applications.closedReason, and 4 more. applications.status has NO constraint despite being the 20-state workflow spine.
impact: 13 of 236 enum-shaped columns are guarded = 5.5%. The unguarded 223 accept any string, so a typo'd status persists silently and is only caught by application code. Concretely: applications.closedReason IS constrained but applications.status — the column every workflow transition writes — is not, which is the wrong way round. Note the honest limit: I found no invalid values in the live data, so this is prospective risk, not present corruption, and the DB is small (10 applications).
fix: Do not convert to Postgres ENUM — the team's text+CHECK pattern is the better choice here (adding a value to a CHECK is a cheap DROP/ADD; ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE cannot run inside a transaction on older PG and cannot remove values at all). Extend the existing pattern instead, highest-value first: `ALTER TABLE applications ADD CONSTRAINT applications_status_check CHECK (status = ANY (ARRAY[...20 states...])) NOT VALID;` then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` in a second statement — NOT VALID makes it non-blocking on a live table. Generate the value list from the workflow constants so it cannot drift. Repeat for invoices.status and payment_transactions.status only after SCH-04 settles the casing. Tier C = operator merge.

Better root fix: stop citing line numbers in schema comments at all (they rot on every edit); cite function names, which grep finds.

title: An overturned document verdict leaves no timestamp and no audit row
evidence: The route upserts on the unique key (applicationId, slotId, round). Its `update` branch (:250-255) overwrites verdict, reason, dueDate and reviewerId. The live table application_document_reviews has columns id, applicationId, slot_id, verdict, reason, due_date, reviewer_id, round, created_at, organization_id — created_at only, no updatedAt (confirmed: it is one of the 28). So an overturn keeps the ORIGINAL created_at while swapping in the new reviewer's id. `grep -nE 'audit|Audit' routes/api/provider/document-reviews.js` returns only 3 comment lines — no safeAudit/auditLog call on this write path.
impact: When officer B reverses officer A's ACCEPTED to MORE_REQUESTED, the row reads as though officer B decided it at officer A's timestamp, and nothing anywhere records that a reversal happened. On a government certification platform this is the one table whose history a challenge would subpoena. Distinguish from the other 27: this one is genuinely broken, most are not (see notes).
fix: Two parts, both small. (1) Schema: add `updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt @map("updated_at")` to prisma/schema/application-document-review.prisma — additive, no backfill needed, expand-only. (2) Route: add a safeAudit('DOC_REVIEW_VERDICT_CHANGED', ...) call after the upsert when the returned row's verdict differs from the pre-read value, mirroring the pattern purchase-invoice-service.js:714-730 already uses. Tier C (schema + governance).

title: Two live-routed models for one finance document — quotes (0 rows) and quotations (3 rows)
evidence: Both tables exist live: quotes has 0 rows, quotations has 3. Both are mounted: routes/api/finance/quotes.js:32 and routes/api/helpers/quotes-provider-routes.js:14 both require services/quote-service.js, and `prisma.quote.`/`tx.quote.` appears 29 times across 6 files (accounting-service.js, quote-service.js, preview-financial-utils.js, and the two route files) versus 2 references to `prisma.quotation.`. They even disagree on vocabulary: quotes.status `@default("pending")` with pending/accepted/rejected/expired (billing.prisma:283) against quotations.status `@default("DRAFT")` with DRAFT|SENT|ACCEPTED|REJECTED|EXPIRED|INVOICED (:753).
impact: The empty legacy model has 14x the code references of the model that actually holds data, and an operator ruling already fixed the finance document set at three types, not four. Any new finance work has a 50% chance of extending the dead one — and a reviewer reading accounting-service.js cannot tell which table backs a revenue number without checking row counts.
fix: Read-only inventory first, deletion second — the platform is pre-production with no historical data to preserve, so this is a clean delete rather than a deprecation. Step 1 (no risk): confirm with the operator which model the three-document ruling designates canonical; the row counts and the newer uppercase vocabulary both point to `quotations`. Step 2: retire services/quote-service.js and the two route files, repoint accounting-service.js and preview-financial-utils.js at quotation, then drop the quotes table in a contract migration. >10 files touched — smallest correct first move is Step 1 plus a BACKLOG entry; the sweep is a follow-up. Tier C (money + schema) = operator merge.

title: Naming is 98.8% camelCase — and the two exceptions are the newest tables, not legacy SQL
evidence: Across 1889 non-Prisma-internal columns: 1445 camelCase, 426 single-word (no style expressed), 18 snake_case. Only 3 tables mix the two, and one is a false positive — users' two 'snake' columns are idCard_deprecated and idCardHash_deprecated, a deliberate deprecation suffix. The genuine mixers are checkout_orders (11 snake / 10 camel — total_payable_amount, dtam_fee_amount, platform_fee_net/vat/gross, quotation_id, payment_terms_accepted_at, payment_terms_version, quotation_snapshot_hash, dtam_remittance_status, stripe_payment_intent_id) and application_document_reviews (5 snake / 1 camel). Both are recent tables, and both reach snake_case via explicit @map: application-document-review.prisma:19-42 maps every field, billing.prisma:1320 `dtamPayableAmount Decimal @db.Decimal(15,2) @map("dtam_fee_amount")`.
impact: This inverts the usual hypothesis: the snake_case is NOT hand-written legacy SQL, it is new Prisma models that chose a different convention via @map. Cost is confined to raw SQL and psql work — a query against checkout_orders must quote "applicationId" but not total_payable_amount, in the same WHERE clause. It is the money table and the review table, so those are the two people hand-query most. Prisma callers are unaffected: field names are camelCase everywhere.
fix: Do not rename existing columns — renaming checkout_orders columns is a Tier C money migration whose only benefit is aesthetic, and billing.prisma:1319 already records that renaming dtam_fee_amount is separately filed. Fix the direction instead: add the convention to CLAUDE.md or HARNESS.md in one line — 'new Prisma models use camelCase columns; @map only to preserve an existing physical name' — and enforce with a probe that fails when a NEW migration introduces a snake_case column. That prevents table 3 and 4 at zero risk to tables 1 and 2.

title: applications is 74 columns wide and carries three retired-but-live column pairs
evidence: applications is the widest table at 74 columns (users 73, certificates 66, invoices 43). It holds three duplicate pairs: totalAreaTypes + cultivationScopeCount, certificationPurpose + certificationPurposes, and phase1SlipId + phase2SlipId. phase-flow.js:135-140 documents the first as an in-flight expand: 'Retired name for the same number, patched in step so a process still serving the previous image prices correctly; the contract migration drops it.' Live check of the fee-input pair: 7 of 10 rows 'diverge', but the divergence is entirely totalAreaTypes=1 / cultivationScopeCount=NULL on DRAFT rows never priced; all 3 rows that reached a priced status (PENDING_DOC_FEE, AUDIT_PASSED) have both = 3. Slip columns: 0 rows non-null, and payment-by-slip is a retired flow. certificationPurpose 5 non-null vs certificationPurposes 10.
impact: No live defect — I specifically tested whether the duplicated FEE INPUT had diverged in a way that would mis-price, and it has not: the writer sets both in step (phase-flow.js:135-140) and every priced row agrees. The cost is the contract half of expand-then-contract never landing: each retired column is a live footgun for the next author, and the phase1*/phase2* doubling (Amount/Status/PaidAt/ExpiresAt/InvoiceId/SlipId = 12 columns) is why the table is 74 wide.
fix: Contract migrations, one per pair, smallest first and each independently revertible. Free one now: `ALTER TABLE applications DROP COLUMN "phase1SlipId", DROP COLUMN "phase2SlipId"` — 0 rows affected, flow retired, no drain needed. Then totalAreaTypes once every deployed image writes cultivationScopeCount (verify via the phase-flow patch having drained). Leave certificationPurpose/Purposes until someone confirms the singular is not still read. Do NOT collapse the phase1/phase2 columns into a child table — that is a money-path refactor with no defect behind it. Tier C = operator merge.

title: 379 timestamp columns are 'without time zone' against 3 timestamptz — safe today only because the DB happens to be UTC
where: live DB information_schema (379 timestamp, 3 timestamptz, 124 with defaults)
evidence: Column type census: text 1136, timestamp 379, bool 101, int4 99, float8 64, jsonb 63, numeric 34, uuid 10, varchar 5, timestamptz 3. So 99.2% of temporal columns are `timestamp without time zone`. I checked the two things that decide whether this is harmful: `current_setting('TimeZone')` on the live pooler session returns UTC, and 124 of those columns carry a DEFAULT. Prisma's DateTime maps to timestamp(3) and Prisma always reads and writes UTC, so Prisma-written values and now()-defaulted values currently agree.
impact: Honest assessment: no present bug, and I could not construct one — DB session tz is UTC and Prisma is UTC, so the two writer classes agree. The exposure is that nothing enforces it. Any raw SQL run from a session with TimeZone=Asia/Bangkok writes values 7 hours off into the same column, and the column type cannot tell you it happened. That matters more than usual here because deadlines are computed on Thai business days (correction dueAt, invoice dueDate, revisionDue) where a 7-hour skew crosses a date boundary and moves a legal deadline by a day.
fix: Do not convert 379 columns — that is a rewrite of every table for a bug that is not occurring. Cheapest real protection, in order: (1) pin the session — add `?options=-c%20TimeZone%3DUTC` to the connection string or `SET TIME ZONE 'UTC'` in the pool's on-connect hook, so the assumption this all rests on is enforced rather than inherited; (2) add a probe asserting current_setting('TimeZone')='UTC' against the live DB, so a Supabase-side default change fails a gate instead of silently skewing deadlines. Convert to timestamptz only for genuinely new deadline columns going forward.

title: Money is stored in three representations across the system — numeric(15,2), int4 satang, and int4 baht
evidence: Full sweep of money-shaped columns. The finance ledger is uniformly numeric(15,2) — invoices, invoice_line_items, quotations, quotes, credit_notes, debit_notes, purchase_invoices, journal_entries, journal_lines, checkout_orders, dtam_remittance_batches, subscriptions: 31 columns, all precision 15 scale 2, no exceptions. Against that: payment_transactions.amount is int4 in SATANG (billing.prisma:327-335, explicit); applications.phase1Amount/phase2Amount are int4 in BAHT; payment_slips.amountClaimed/amountVerified are int4 in WHOLE BAHT with a 20-line warning at billing.prisma:447-455 recording a past incident where a stray /100 'was understating every verified amount 100x'.
impact: The numeric(15,2) core is correct and consistent — this is the part of the schema most likely to be right, and it is. The risk is entirely at the three boundaries where units change: satang↔baht↔decimal. The schema documents each boundary but the documentation is what rotted in SCH-06, and the 100x incident at billing.prisma:447-455 is what a missed conversion costs. payment_slips is additionally a retired flow (0 rows, slip payment removed).
fix: No type changes — converting payment_transactions.amount off satang would break Stripe's own integer contract, and numeric(15,2) is already right. Make the boundary mechanical instead: the codebase already has `toSatang()` (used at stripe-checkout-service.js:683) but phase-flow.js:217 open-codes `* 100`. Route both through toSatang/fromSatang and forbid bare `* 100` / `/ 100` on money via the existing eslint-rules/ directory. Separately, drop payment_slips.amountClaimed/amountVerified with the retired slip flow (0 rows). Tier C, propose only — I ran no writes.

title: Four unindexed foreign keys — real, but genuinely noise against a 244ms round trip
evidence: The four app-owned unindexed FKs from the measurements, checked against live row counts: application_document_reviews 11 rows, application_documents 53 rows, correction_rounds 0 rows, correction_submission_versions 0 rows. Notably all four are on the newest tables — the same cohort as the snake_case exceptions in SCH-09 and the missing updatedAt in SCH-07.
impact: Ranked honestly by measured user cost: at these row counts Postgres will seq-scan in well under 1ms, against a 244ms Sydney round trip that every query pays regardless. Adding these indexes today would save approximately nothing — roughly 0.4% of one query's cost at best, and two of the tables are empty. The reason to act is not latency, it is that a missing FK index turns every parent DELETE into a full scan of the child, and organization_id is the tenant-scoping column that RLS enforcement will filter on in Phases 1-3.
fix: Low priority, batch with the next schema PR rather than its own: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on each of the four (CONCURRENTLY so it never takes a write lock, and it cannot run inside a transaction so it needs its own migration file). Do this before RLS enforcement lands, not before — the tenant filter is what makes organization_id hot. Explicitly do NOT prioritise this over SCH-01/02: an index that saves microseconds is worth less than a tax report that returns the right rows.
